claims.text: Introducing an intermediate-temperature dwell enhances atomic mixing during nanoparticle nucleation.
Enhanced atomic mixing suppresses elemental segregation.
Enhanced atomic mixing promotes formation of a single-phase solid solution.
Rapid heating and cooling without an intermediate hold typically produces nonuniform atomic distributions or phase separation in the targeted noble-metal nanoparticles.
The dwell can be varied while composition and chemical environment are held constant.
Rapid HEA-nanoparticle synthesis can use peak temperatures near 2000 K followed by very rapid cooling.
High reaction temperatures followed by rapid cooling can preserve a single solid-solution high-entropy state by suppressing secondary phases.
More than five near-equimolar noble metals provide the high configurational entropy required by the proposed regime.
Excessive dwell duration can induce particle growth, decomposition, or unwanted phase transitions.
An intermediate-temperature dwell increases atomic mobility.
Increased atomic mobility during the dwell enables more homogeneous diffusion of the constituent metals before crystallization.
Subsequent rapid crystallization locks the homogenized atomic distribution into the nanoparticle structure.
A rapid heating-cooling profile traps local concentration fluctuations and thereby causes phase separation and elemental segregation.
The dwell-induced mixing reduces local lattice distortions and suppresses elemental clustering.
Relative to the no-dwell baseline, dwell-treated nanoparticles will have a more uniform elemental distribution and greater single-phase solid-solution retention.
EDS elemental mapping can assess the homogeneity of elemental distributions in an alloy.
X-ray diffraction can be used to identify alloy phase structure and phase transitions.
The optimal intermediate temperature and dwell duration vary with precursor chemistry and nanoparticle size.
The peak temperature must be high enough to decompose the precursors.

contradictions.description: The baseline is described as elementally inhomogeneous and potentially phase-separated, whereas the outcome says the intervention will 'retain' a single-phase structure and the falsification rule asks whether the single-phase structure is unchanged relative to that baseline. It is therefore unclear whether the baseline is single-phase, phase-separated, or merely at risk of phase separation.
